documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: Avogadro's number
problems.statement: Spherical water droplets are dispersed in argon gas. At $27\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, each droplet is $1.0$ micrometer in diameter and undergoes collisions with argon. Assume that inter-droplet collisions do not occur. The root-mean-square speed of these droplets was determined to be $0.50\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$ at $27\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The density of a water droplet is $1.0\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.

parts.statement:
Calculate the average kinetic energy ($mv^2/2$) of this droplet at $27\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The volume of a sphere is $(4/3)\pi r^3$, where $r$ is the radius.

If the temperature is changed, then droplet size and speed will also change. The average kinetic energy of a droplet between $0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ as a function of temperature is found to be linear. Assume that it remains linear below $0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

![](p1-fig1)

At thermal equilibrium, the average kinetic energy is the same irrespective of particle masses (equipartition theorem). The specific heat capacity, at constant volume, of argon gas (atomic weight, 40) is $0.31\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.
Calculate Avogadro's number without using the ideal gas law, the gas constant, or Boltzmann's constant.

sections.statement:
The mass of a water droplet:

$$m=V\rho=\left(\frac43\pi r^3\right)\rho=\frac43\pi(0.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m})^3(1.0\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}})=5.2\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{kg}.$$

The printed average kinetic-energy substitution at $27\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is

$$E_k=\frac{mv^2}2=\frac{(5.2\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{kg})(0.51\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m/s})^2}2=6.9\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2/s^2}=6.9\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}.$$

The average kinetic energy of an argon atom is the same as that of a water droplet. $E_k$ becomes zero at $-273\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. From the linear relationship in the figure, $E_k=aT$ (absolute temperature), where $a$ is the increase in kinetic energy of an argon atom per degree.

$$a=\frac{E_k}T=\frac{6.9\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}}{(27+273)\ \mathrm{K}}=2.3\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}.$$

$S$: specific heat of argon. $N$: number of atoms in $1\ \mathrm{g}$ of argon.

$$S=0.31\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}=aN,\qquad N=\frac Sa=\frac{0.31\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}}{2.3\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}}=1.4\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{g^{-1}}.$$

Avogadro's number is the number of argon atoms in $40\ \mathrm{g}$ of argon:

$$N_A=40\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\times1.4\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{g^{-1}}=5.6\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}.$$

### Source notes

The question gives $0.50\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$, while the printed key substitutes $0.51\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Its numerical energy and final Avogadro value are retained literally, without correcting the source.

problems.title: Detection of hydrogen
problems.statement: Hydrogen is prevalent in the universe. Life in the universe is ultimately based on hydrogen.

parts.statement:
There are about $1\times10^{23}$ stars in the universe. Assume that they are like our sun: radius $700{,}000\ \mathrm{km}$, density $1.4\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, $3/4$ hydrogen and $1/4$ helium by mass. Estimate the number of stellar protons in the universe to one significant figure.

In the 1920s Cecilia Payne discovered by spectral analysis of starlight that hydrogen is the most abundant element in most stars.

The electronic transition of a hydrogen atom is governed by

$$\Delta E(n_i\to n_f)=-C\left(\frac1{n_f^2}-\frac1{n_i^2}\right),$$

where $n$ is principle quantum number and $C$ a constant. For detection of the $\Delta E(3\to2)$ transition ($656.3\ \mathrm{nm}$ in the Balmer series), the electron in the ground state of the hydrogen atom needs first to be excited to $n=2$. Calculate the wavelength (in nm) of the absorption line in starlight corresponding to the $\Delta E(1\to2)$ transition.

According to Wien's law, the wavelength $\lambda$ corresponding to the maximum light intensity emitted from a blackbody at temperature $T$ is given by $\lambda T=2.9\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m\,K}$. Calculate the surface temperature of a star whose blackbody radiation has a peak intensity corresponding to the $n=1\to n=2$ excitation of hydrogen.

The ground state of hydrogen is split into two hyperfine levels due to interaction between the magnetic moment of the proton and that of the electron. In 1951, Purcell discovered a spectral line at $1420\ \mathrm{MHz}$ due to the hyperfine transition of hydrogen in interstellar space.

Hydrogen in interstellar space cannot be excited electronically by starlight. However, the cosmic background radiation, equivalent to $2.7\ \mathrm{K}$, can cause the hyperfine transition. Calculate the temperature of a blackbody whose peak intensity corresponds to the $1420\ \mathrm{MHz}$ transition.

Wien generated hydrogen ions by discharge of hydrogen gas at a very low pressure and determined the $e/m$ value, which turned out to be the highest among different gases tested. In 1919, Rutherford bombarded nitrogen with alpha-particles and observed emission of a positively charged particle which turned out to be the hydrogen ion observed by Wien. Rutherford named this particle the “proton”. Fill in the blank.

sections.statement:
$$\text{Mass of a typical star}=\frac43(3.1)(7\times10^8\ \mathrm{m})^3(1.4\times10^6\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-3}})=2\times10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}.$$

$$\text{Mass of protons of a typical star}=(2\times10^{33}\ \mathrm{g})\left(\frac34+\frac18\right)=1.8\times10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}.$$

$$\text{Number of protons of a typical star}=(1.8\times10^{33}\ \mathrm{g})(6\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{g^{-1}})=1\times10^{57}.$$

$$\text{Number of stellar protons in the universe}=(1\times10^{57})(10^{23})=1\times10^{80}.$$

problems.statementAfterParts:
### Source notes

Question 2.5 says “Fill in the blank”, but the collection prints no corresponding blank reaction scheme before the solution. The printed key is retained without inventing the absent question layout. Key 2.2 labels the $656.3\ \mathrm{nm}$ transition as $2\to3$, while the question uses $3\to2$. Key 2.4 prints the numerator unit m, without /s, and that literal substitution is retained.

problems.title: Interstellar chemistry
problems.statement:
Early interstellar chemistry is thought to have been a prelude to life on Earth. Molecules can be formed in space via heterogeneous reactions at the surface of dust particles, often called interstellar ice grains (IIGs). Imagine the reaction between H and C atoms on the IIG surface that forms CH. The CH product can either be desorbed from the surface or further react through surface migration with adsorbed H atoms to form $\mathrm{CH_2}$, $\mathrm{CH_3}$, etc.

Depending on how energetically a molecule “jumps” from its anchored site, it either leaves the surface permanently (desorption) or returns to a new position at the surface (migration). The rates of desorption and migratory jump follow the Arrhenius formula $k=A\exp(-E/RT)$, where $k$ is the rate constant for desorption or migratory jump, $A$ the jumping frequency, and $E$ the activation energy for the respective event.

parts.statement: Desorption of CH from the IIG surface follows first-order kinetics. Calculate the average residence time of CH on the surface at $20\ \mathrm{K}$. Assume $A=1\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $E_{des}=12\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

Consider the shortest time it would take for one CH unit to move from its initial position to the opposite side of an IIG by successive migratory jumps. Assume that the activation energy for migration $E_{mig}=6\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, and that the IIG is a sphere with radius $0.1\ \mathrm{\mu m}$. Each migratory jump laterally advances the molecule by $0.3\ \mathrm{nm}$. Show work and choose your answer from (a)–(e).

- (a) $t\leq1$ day.
- (b) $10$ days $\leq t\leq10^2$ yr.
- (c) $10^3$ yr $\leq t\leq10^6$ yr.
- (d) $10^7$ yr $\leq t\leq10^{10}$ yr.
- (e) $t\geq10^{11}$ yr.

Consider the reaction of CO with $\mathrm{H_2}$ to form $\mathrm{H_2CO}$. The activation energy on a metal catalyst is $20\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ that is produced by formaldehyde at a rate of $1$ molecule/s per site at $300\ \mathrm{K}$. Estimate the rate of formaldehyde formation per site if the reaction takes place at $20\ \mathrm{K}$.

Which is a set of all true statements? Circle one.

- (a) Most CH species are desorbed from the IIG surface before encountering other reactants by surface migration.
- (b) IIGs can assist transformation of simple molecules to more complex ones in interstellar space.
- (c) For a reaction on the IIG to occur at an appreciable speed during the age of the Universe ($1\times10^{10}$ yr), the reaction energy barrier must be absent or negligible.

Choices: □ (a), □ (b), □ (c), □ (a, b), □ (a, c), □ (b, c), □ (a, b, c).

sections.statement:
At $T=20\ \mathrm{K}$:

$$k_{des}=A\exp(-E_{des}/RT)=(1\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}})(5\times10^{-32})=5\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.$$

Surface residence time:

$$T_{residence}=\frac1{k_{des}}=2\times10^{19}\ \mathrm{s}=6\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{yr}.$$

Full credit for $T_{half-life}=\ln2/k_{des}=1\times10^{19}\ \mathrm{s}=4\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{yr}$. Residence time $=2\times10^{19}\ \mathrm{s}$.

The distance traveled is $x=\pi r=300\ \mathrm{nm}$.

$$k_{mig}=A\exp(-E_{mig}/RT)=(1\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}})(2\times10^{-16})=2\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\quad\text{at }T=20\ \mathrm{K}.$$

Average time between migratory jumps: $T=1/k_{mig}=5\times10^3\ \mathrm{s}$.

$$t=\frac{300\ \mathrm{nm}}{0.3\ \mathrm{nm}}\ \text{jumps}\times5\times10^3\ \mathrm{s/jump}=5\times10^6\ \mathrm{s}=50\ \text{days}.$$

The correct answer is (b).

Full credit for calculation using a random-walk model. In this case,

$$t=T(x/d)^2=5\times10^9\ \mathrm{s}=160\ \mathrm{yr}.$$

The printed key says the answer is still (b).

$$\frac{k(20\ \mathrm{K})}{k(300\ \mathrm{K})}=\exp\left[\frac ER\left(\frac1{T_1}-\frac1{T_2}\right)\right]=e^{-112}\approx1\times10^{-49}.$$

The formaldehyde-production rate at $20\ \mathrm{K}$ is approximately $1\times10^{-49}\ \text{molecule/site/s}$, or approximately $1\times10^{-42}\ \text{molecule/site/yr}$. The reaction will not occur at all during the age of the universe ($1\times10^{10}$ yr).

problems.statementAfterParts:
### Source notes

The key awards full credit to both the residence-time and half-life approaches. It also accepts both the shortest-path and random-walk calculations in 3.2. Its $160$-year random-walk result exceeds the printed option (b) upper bound of $100$ years, but the key still names (b); this contradiction is retained. The printed temperature labels in the 3.3 exponent are not silently reordered.

problems.title: The Chemistry of DNA

parts.statement:
In 1944 Oswald Avery isolated a genetic material and showed by elemental analysis that it was a sodium salt of deoxyribonucleic acid. A segment of DNA with formula mass of $1323.72$ is shown.

![](p4-fig1)

Assuming that equimolar amounts of the four bases are present in DNA, write the number of H atoms per P atom. Calculate, to three significant figures, the theoretical weight percentage of H expected upon elemental analysis of DNA.

Chargaff extracted the separated bases and determined their concentrations by measuring UV absorbance. The Beer-Lambert law was used to obtain the molar concentration. Chargaff discovered the following molar ratios for bases in DNA:

| Ratio | Value |
|---|---|
| Adenine to guanine | 1.43 |
| Thymine to cytosine | 1.43 |
| Adenine to thymine | 1.02 |
| Guanine to cytosine | 1.02 |

Chargaff's discovery suggested that the bases might exist as pairs in DNA. Watson and Crick mentioned in their celebrated 1953 paper in *Nature*: “It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.”

Draw structures of the specific pairing found in DNA. Indicate hydrogen bonds. Omit the sugar-phosphate backbone.
Mutation can occur through base pairings different from the above. Draw structures of any three alternative base pairs.

The plausibility of formation of purine and pyrimidine bases in the prebiotic atmosphere of the Earth from $\mathrm{HCN}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$, and $\mathrm{H_2O}$ has been demonstrated in the laboratory. Write the minimum number of HCN and $\mathrm{H_2O}$ molecules required for formation of the following compounds.

![](p4-fig2)

problems.title: Acid-Base Chemistry

parts.statement: Calculate $[\mathrm{H^+}]$, $[\mathrm{OH^-}]$, $[\mathrm{HSO_4^-}]$, and $[\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}]$ in a $1.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{M}$ solution of sulfuric acid. $K_w=1.0\times10^{-14}$ and $K_2=1.2\times10^{-2}$ at $25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. You may use mass- and charge-balance equations. Answer with two significant figures.

Calculate the volume of $0.80\ \mathrm{M}$ NaOH solution that should be added to a $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ aqueous solution containing $3.48\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of concentrated phosphoric acid to prepare a pH 7.4 buffer. Answer with three significant figures.

$\mathrm{H_3PO_4(aq)}$: purity $85$ mass %, density $1.69\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$, $M_r=98.00$. $\mathrm{p}K_1=2.15$, $\mathrm{p}K_2=7.20$, $\mathrm{p}K_3=12.44$.

The efficacy of a drug is greatly dependent on its ability to be absorbed into the blood stream. Acid-base chemistry plays an important role in drug absorption.

![](p5-fig1)

Assume that the ionic form $\mathrm{A^-}$ of a weakly acidic drug does not penetrate the membrane, whereas the neutral form HA freely crosses it. Also assume equilibrium is established so that the concentration of HA is the same on both sides. Calculate the ratio of the total concentration $[\mathrm{HA}]+[\mathrm{A^-}]$ of aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid, $\mathrm{p}K=3.52$) in blood to that in the stomach.

sections.statement:
First ionization is complete:

$$\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\longrightarrow\mathrm{H^+}+\mathrm{HSO_4^-},\qquad[\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]=0.$$

Second ionization:

$$\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}]}{[\mathrm{HSO_4^-}]}=K_2=1.2\times10^{-2}\qquad(1).$$

Mass balance:

$$[\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]+[\mathrm{HSO_4^-}]+[\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}]=1.0\times10^{-7}\qquad(2).$$

Charge balance:

$$[\mathrm{H^+}]=[\mathrm{HSO_4^-}]+2[\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}]+[\mathrm{OH^-}]\qquad(3).$$

Degree of ionization increases on dilution. $[\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]=0$. Assume $[\mathrm{H^+}]_{\mathrm{H_2SO_4}}=2\times10^{-7}$. From (1), $[\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}]/[\mathrm{HSO_4^-}]=6\times10^4$, so second ionization is almost complete and $[\mathrm{HSO_4^-}]=0$. From (2), $[\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}]=1.0\times10^{-7}$.

From (3),

$$[\mathrm{H^+}]=2\times10^{-7}+\frac{10^{-14}}{[\mathrm{H^+}]},\qquad[\mathrm{H^+}]=2.4\times10^{-7}\quad(\mathrm{pH}=6.6),$$

$$[\mathrm{OH^-}]=\frac{1\times10^{-14}}{2.4\times10^{-7}}=4.1\times10^{-8}.$$

From (1),

$$[\mathrm{HSO_4^-}]=\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}]}{K_2}=\frac{(2.4\times10^{-7})(1.0\times10^{-7})}{1.2\times10^{-2}}=2.0\times10^{-12}.$$

Check charge balance:

$$2.4\times10^{-7}\approx2.0\times10^{-12}+2(1.0\times10^{-7})+4.1\times10^{-8}.$$

Check mass balance:

$$0+2.0\times10^{-12}+1.0\times10^{-7}\approx1.0\times10^{-7}.$$

$$n(\mathrm{H_3PO_4})=0.85\times3.48\ \mathrm{cm^3}\times1.69\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\times\frac{1\ \mathrm{mol}}{98.00\ \mathrm{g}}\times1000=51.0\ \mathrm{mmol}.$$

The desired pH is above $\mathrm{p}K_2$. A 1:1 mixture of $\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}$ and $\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}$ would have $\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm{p}K_2=7.20$. For pH 7.40 there must be more $\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}$. Add NaOH to convert $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$ to $\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}$ and the right amount of $\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}$ to $\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}$.

The two reactions printed on the first key page are

$$\mathrm{H_3PO_4}+\mathrm{OH^-}\longrightarrow\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}+\mathrm{H_2O},$$

$$\mathrm{H_2PO_4}+\mathrm{OH^-}\longrightarrow\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}+\mathrm{H_2O}.$$

The volume of $0.80$ NaOH needed to convert $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$ to $\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}$ is

$$51.0\ \mathrm{mmol}\div0.80\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}=63.75\ \mathrm{cm^3}.$$

To obtain pH 7.40:

$$\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}+\mathrm{OH^-}\longrightarrow\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}.$$

| mmol | $\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}$ | $\mathrm{OH^-}$ | $\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial | 51.0 | $x$ | 0 |
| Final | $51.0-x$ | 0 | $x$ |

$$\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm{p}K_2+\log\frac{[\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}]}{[\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}]},\qquad7.40=7.20+\log\frac{x}{51.0-x},\qquad x=31.27\ \mathrm{mmol}.$$

$$V=31.27\ \mathrm{mmol}\div0.80\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}=39.09\ \mathrm{cm^3}.$$

Total NaOH volume $=63.75+39.09=102.84\ \mathrm{cm^3}\approx103\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.

$\mathrm{p}K=3.52$.

$$\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm{p}K_a+\log\frac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]},\qquad\frac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}=10^{\mathrm{pH}-\mathrm{p}K_a}.$$

In blood, pH 7.40:

$$[\mathrm{A^-}]/[\mathrm{HA}]=10^{7.40-3.52}=7586,\qquad\text{Total ASA}=7586+1=7587.$$

In stomach, pH 2.00:

$$[\mathrm{A^-}]/[\mathrm{HA}]=10^{2.00-3.52}=3.02\times10^{-2},\qquad\text{Total ASA}=1+3.02\times10^{-2}=1.03.$$

Ratio of total aspirin in blood to stomach $=7587/1.03=7400$.

problems.title: Electrochemistry
problems.statement: Water is a very stable molecule, abundant on earth and essential for life. As such, water was long thought to be a chemical element. Soon after the invention of a voltaic cell in 1800, Nicholson and Carlyle decomposed water into hydrogen and oxygen by electrolysis.

parts.statement: Water can be thought of as hydrogen oxidized by oxygen. Thus, hydrogen can be recovered by reduction of water, using an aqueous solution of sodium sulfate, at a platinum electrode connected to the negative terminal of a battery. The solution near the electrode becomes basic. Write a balanced half-reaction for the reduction of water.

Water can also be thought of as oxygen reduced by hydrogen. Thus, oxygen can be recovered by oxidation of water at the Pt electrode connected to the positive terminal. Write a balanced half-reaction for oxidation of water.

When copper is used at both electrodes, gas is generated only at one electrode during the initial stage of electrolysis. Write the half-reaction at the electrode that does not generate gas.

Another species in solution that can be reduced is sodium ion. Reduction to metallic sodium does not occur in aqueous solution because water is reduced first. However, as Humphrey Davy discovered in 1807, sodium can be made by electrolysis of fused sodium chloride.

Based on these observations, connect the half-reactions with the standard reduction potential (in volts). The columns below are the **unconnected native question columns**, not matched answers.

| Half-reaction | Potential choices in printed order |
|---|---|
| Reduction of copper ion ($\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$) | $+0.340$ |
| Reduction of oxygen | $-2.710$ |
| Reduction of water | $-0.830$ |
| Reduction of sodium ion ($\mathrm{Na^+}$) | $0.000$ |
| Reduction of hydrogen ion | $+1.230$ |

The electrode potential is affected by other reactions near the electrode. The potential of the $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}$ electrode in $0.100\ \mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ solution changes as $\mathrm{Cu(OH)_2}$ precipitates. Answer the following problems with three significant figures. Temperature is $25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$; $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$.
Precipitation of $\mathrm{Cu(OH)_2}$ begins at pH 4.84. Determine its solubility product.
Calculate the standard reduction potential for $\mathrm{Cu(OH)_2(s)}+2\mathrm{e^-}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Cu(s)}+2\mathrm{OH^-}$.

Calculate the electrode potential at pH 1.00.

Lithium cobalt oxide and specialty carbon are active ingredients for the positive and negative electrodes, respectively, of a rechargeable lithium battery. During the charge-recharge cycles, the following reversible half-reactions occur:

$$\mathrm{LiCoO_2}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{Li_{1-x}CoO_2}+x\mathrm{Li^+}+x\mathrm{e^-},$$

$$\mathrm C+x\mathrm{Li^+}+x\mathrm{e^-}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{CLi_x}.$$

The total amount of energy a battery can store is rated in mAh. A battery rated at $1500\ \mathrm{mAh}$ can power a device drawing $100$ milliamps for $15$ hours.

Graphite has lithium intercalation sites between its layers. Assuming a maximum $6:1$ carbon-to-lithium intercalation stoichiometry, calculate the theoretical charge capacity of $1.00\ \mathrm{g}$ graphite to intercalate lithium. Answer in mAh/g with three significant figures.

sections.statement:
Reduction of sodium ion seldom takes place; it has a highly negative reduction potential of $-2.710\ \mathrm V$. The potential for water to hydrogen is negative (water is very stable), but not as negative as for sodium ion: $-0.830\ \mathrm V$. Reduction of copper ion and oxygen occurs readily, and both potentials are positive. In this system, the reverse reaction (oxidation) occurs at the positive terminal. Copper is oxidized before water. The hydrogen-ion reduction potential is defined as $0.000\ \mathrm V$.

![](p6-sol-fig1)

$$
\begin{aligned}
E&=E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu})+\frac{0.0592}2\log[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]\\
&=+0.340+\frac{0.0592}2\log\frac{K_{sp}}{[\mathrm{OH^-}]^2}\\
&=+0.340+\frac{0.0592}2\log K_{sp}-\frac{0.0592}2\log[\mathrm{OH^-}]^2\\
&=+0.340+\frac{0.0592}2\log K_{sp}-0.0592\log[\mathrm{OH^-}].
\end{aligned}
$$

By definition, the standard potential for $\mathrm{Cu(OH)_2(s)}+2\mathrm{e^-}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Cu(s)}+2\mathrm{OH^-}$ is the potential where $[\mathrm{OH^-}]=1.00$.

$$E=E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu(OH)_2/Cu})=+0.340+\frac{0.0592}2\log K_{sp}=+0.340+\frac{0.0592}2\log(4.79\times10^{-20})=+0.340-0.572=-0.232\ \mathrm V.$$

**Alternative printed method:**

Equation 1: $\mathrm{Cu(OH)_2(s)}+2\mathrm{e^-}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Cu}+2\mathrm{OH^-}$, with $E_+^\circ=E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu(OH)_2/Cu})=?$.

Equation 2: $\mathrm{Cu(OH)_2(s)}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}+2\mathrm{OH^-}$.

$$E^\circ=\frac{0.05916}{n}\log K_{sp}=\frac{0.05916}2\log(4.79\times10^{-20})=-0.5715\ \mathrm V.$$

Equation 1 minus Equation 2: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}+2\mathrm{e^-}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Cu}$, so

$$E_-^\circ=E_+^\circ-E^\circ=E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu})=0.34\ \mathrm V.$$

Therefore $E_+^\circ=E_-^\circ+E^\circ=+0.34+(-0.5715)=-0.232\ \mathrm V$.

Below pH 4.84 there is no effect of $\mathrm{Cu(OH)_2}$ because no precipitation occurs. Therefore

$$E=E(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu})=+0.340+\frac{0.0592}2\log[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]=+0.340+\frac{0.0592}2\log0.100=+0.340-0.0296=+0.310\ \mathrm V.$$

$1.00\ \mathrm g$ graphite is $0.0833\ \mathrm{mol}$ carbon. With $6$ mol carbon to $1$ mol lithium, $1\ \mathrm g$ graphite can hold $0.0139\ \mathrm{mol}$ lithium. Inserting $1$ mol lithium requires $96487$ coulombs. Thus $1\ \mathrm g$ graphite can charge $96487\times0.0139=1340$ coulombs.

$$1340\ \mathrm{C/g}=1340\ \mathrm{A\,s/g}=1340\times1000\ \mathrm{mA}\times\frac1{3600}\ \mathrm h=372\ \mathrm{mAh/g}.$$

problems.title: Hydrogen Economy
problems.statement: Hydrogen is more energy-dense than carbon, by mass. Historically there has been a move toward fuel with higher hydrogen content: coal → oil → natural gas → hydrogen. Cost-effective production and safe storage are two major hurdles to a hydrogen economy.

parts.statement: Consider hydrogen in a cylinder at $80\ \mathrm{MPa}$ and $25\ ^\circ\mathrm C$. Using the ideal gas law, estimate its density in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

Calculate the ratio between heat generated when hydrogen is burned and heat generated when the same weight of carbon is burned. The difference comes to a large extent from the fact that the most abundant isotope of hydrogen has no neutron and hydrogen has no inner electron shell.

$\Delta H_f^\circ[\mathrm{H_2O(l)}]=-286\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$; $\Delta H_f^\circ[\mathrm{CO_2(g)}]=-394\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

Calculate the theoretical maximum work produced by combustion of $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ hydrogen (a) from an electric motor using a hydrogen fuel cell and (b) from a heat engine working between $25\ ^\circ\mathrm C$ and $300\ ^\circ\mathrm C$. The efficiency (work done/heat absorbed) of an ideal heat engine working between $T_{cold}$ and $T_{hot}$ is $1-T_{cold}/T_{hot}$.

$$S_{298}^\circ[\mathrm{H_2(g)}]=131\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}},\quad S_{298}^\circ[\mathrm{O_2(g)}]=205\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}},\quad S_{298}^\circ[\mathrm{H_2O(l)}]=70\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}.$$

If the fuel cell works at $1\ \mathrm W$ and the standard potential difference, how long will the electric motor run and at what current?

sections.statement:
The first printed reactant is $\mathrm{Hg_2(g)}$:

$$\mathrm{Hg_2(g)}+\frac12\mathrm{O_2(g)}\longrightarrow\mathrm{H_2O(l)},\qquad\Delta H_{rexn-1}=\Delta H_f[\mathrm{H_2O(l)}]=-286\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}=-143\ \mathrm{kJ\,g^{-1}}.$$

$$\mathrm{C(s)}+\mathrm{O_2(g)}\longrightarrow\mathrm{CO_2(g)},\qquad\Delta H_{rexn-2}=\Delta H_f[\mathrm{CO_2(g)}]=-394\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}=-33\ \mathrm{kJ\,g^{-1}}.$$

$$\frac{-\Delta H_{rexn-1}}{-\Delta H_{rexn-2}}=4.3\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{-\Delta H_{rexn-2}}{-\Delta H_{rexn-1}}=0.23.$$

$$\mathrm{H_2(g)}+\frac12\mathrm{O_2(g)}\longrightarrow\mathrm{H_2O(l)},$$

$$\Delta H_c=-286\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}=-143\ \mathrm{kJ\,g^{-1}}=-143\times10^3\ \mathrm{kJ\,kg^{-1}},\qquad\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S,$$

$$\Delta S_c=70-131-205/2=-163.5\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}},$$

$$\Delta G_c=-286\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}+298\ \mathrm K\times163.5\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}=-237\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}=-1.2\times10^5\ \mathrm{kJ\,kg^{-1}}.$$

(a) Electric motor: $W_{max}=\Delta G_c\times1\ \mathrm{kg}=-1.2\times10^5\ \mathrm{kJ}$.

(b) Heat engine:

$$W_{max}=\text{efficiency}\times\Delta H_c=\left(1-\frac{298}{573}\right)(-143\times10^3\ \mathrm{kJ})=-6.9\times10^4\ \mathrm{kJ}.$$

The printed time equation is

$$119\times10^3\ \mathrm{kJ}=1\ \mathrm W\times t(\mathrm{sec}).$$

$$t=1.2\times10^8\ \mathrm s=3.3\times10^4\ \mathrm h=1.4\times10^3\ \mathrm{days}=46\ \mathrm{month}=3.8\ \mathrm{yr}.$$

$$\Delta G=-nFE,$$

where $n$ is the number of electrons involved and $F=96.5\ \mathrm{kC\,mol^{-1}}$. For $\mathrm{H_2(g)}+\frac12\mathrm{O_2(g)}\longrightarrow\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$, $n=2$.

$$E=\frac{-\Delta G}{nF}=\frac{237\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}}{2\times96.5\ \mathrm{kC\,mol^{-1}}}=1.23\ \mathrm V,\qquad I=\frac WE=0.81\ \mathrm A.$$

problems.title: Chemistry of Iron Oxides
problems.statement:
The nucleus of iron is the most stable among all elements and, therefore, iron accumulates at the core of massive red giant stars where nucleosynthesis of many elements essential for life (such as C, N, O, P, S, etc.) takes place. As a result, among heavy elements iron is quite abundant in the universe. Iron is also abundant on Earth.

Development of a technology for reducing iron oxide to iron was a key step in human civilization. Key reactions in the blast furnace are:

$$\mathrm{C(s)}+\mathrm{O_2(g)}\longrightarrow\mathrm{CO_2(g)},\qquad\Delta H^0=-393.51\ \mathrm{kJ(/mol)}\qquad(1),$$

$$\mathrm{CO_2(g)}+\mathrm{C(s)}\longrightarrow2\mathrm{CO(g)},\qquad\Delta H^0=172.46\ \mathrm{kJ(/mol)}\qquad(2),$$

$$\mathrm{Fe_2O_3(s)}+\mathrm{CO(g)}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Fe(s)}+\mathrm{CO_2(g)},\qquad\Delta H^0=?\qquad(3).$$

parts.statement: Indicate the reducing agent in each reaction.

Balance reaction (3) and calculate its equilibrium constant at $1200\ ^\circ\mathrm C$. $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3(s)})=-824.2\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

| Species | $S^\circ$ ($\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$) |
|---|---|
| Fe(s) | 27.28 |
| $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3(s)}$ | 87.40 |
| C(s) | 5.74 |
| CO(g) | 197.674 |
| $\mathrm{CO_2(g)}$ | 213.74 |

In the manufacture of celadon pottery, $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ is partially reduced in a charcoal kiln to mixed oxides of $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$ and $\mathrm{FeO}$. The amount of different oxides seems related to the “mystic” color of celadon ceramics.

![](p8-fig1)

$\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$ (magnetite) itself is a mixed oxide containing $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ and belongs to compounds with general formula $\mathrm{AB_2O_4}$. Oxide ions form a face-centered cubic array. The figure shows oxygens (gray circles) and representative sites for divalent A and trivalent B cations. The dark circle is a tetrahedral site and the white circle an octahedral site.

![](p8-fig2)

How many available octahedral sites for iron ions are there in one $\mathrm{AB_2O_4}$ unit? Certain sites are shared by neighbouring units.

$\mathrm{AB_2O_4}$ can adopt normal- or inverse-spinel structure. In normal spinel, two B ions occupy two octahedral sites and one A occupies one tetrahedral site. In inverse spinel, one of the two B ions occupies a tetrahedral site; the other B and the A ion occupy octahedral sites.
What percentage of available tetrahedral sites is occupied by either $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ or $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ in $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$?

$\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$ has an inverse-spinel structure. Draw the crystal-field splitting pattern of $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and fill out the electrons. Electron pairing energy is greater than the octahedral-field splitting.

sections.statement:
Balanced equation (3):

$$\mathrm{Fe_2O_3(s)}+3\mathrm{CO(g)}\longrightarrow2\mathrm{Fe(s)}+3\mathrm{CO_2(g)}.$$

$$\mathrm{C(s)}+\mathrm{O_2(g)}\longrightarrow\mathrm{CO_2(g)},\qquad\Delta H^0_{(1)}=-393.51\ \mathrm{kJ}=\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{CO_2(g)}),$$

$$\mathrm{CO_2(g)}+\mathrm{C(s)}\longrightarrow2\mathrm{CO(g)},\qquad\Delta H^0_{(2)}=172.46\ \mathrm{kJ}.$$

From (1) and (2):

$$\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{CO(g)})=\frac12\{172.46+(-393.51)\}=-110.525\ \mathrm{kJ}.$$

$$\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3})=-824.2\ \mathrm{kJ},$$

$$\Delta H^0_{(3)}=3\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{CO_2(g)})-\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3})-3\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{CO(g)})=3(-393.51)-(-824.2)-3(-110.525)=-24.8\ \mathrm{kJ}.$$

The literal printed entropy substitution is

$$\Delta S^\circ_{(3)}=(2\times27.28)+(3\times213.74)-7.4-(3\times197.674)=15.36\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}.$$

$$\Delta G^0_{(3)}=\Delta H^0-T\Delta S^0=-24.8\ \mathrm{kJ}-\left(15.36\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\times\frac{1\ \mathrm{kJ}}{1000\ \mathrm J}\times1473.15\ \mathrm K\right)=-47.43\ \mathrm{kJ},$$

$$K=e^{-\Delta G^\circ/RT}=e^{47430\ \mathrm J/(8.314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\times1473.15\ \mathrm K)}=48.$$
One $\mathrm{AB_2O_4}$ unit has $4=1+\frac14\times12$ available octahedral sites.

One face-centered cube in $\mathrm{AB_2O_4}$ represents one $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$ unit here and has 8 available tetrahedral sites. One tetrahedral site should be occupied by one $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ (normal spinel) or one $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ (inverse spinel). Both give $(1/8)\times100\%=12.5\%$ occupancy of available tetrahedral sites.

problems.title: Photolithographic process
problems.statement:
Photolithography is a process used in semiconductor device fabrication to transfer a pattern from a photomask to the surface of a substrate. In a typical process, light is projected through a mask defining a particular circuitry onto a silicon wafer coated with a thin photoresist layer.

The earliest photoresists were based on photochemistry generating reactive intermediates from bis(aryl azide). Patterning becomes possible through cross-linking of nitrenes generated from the azides.

![](p9-fig1)

parts.statement: Draw two possible Lewis structures of $\mathrm{CH_3-N_3}$, the simplest compound having the same active functional group as bis(aryl azide). Assign formal charges.
Draw the Lewis structure of nitrene expected from $\mathrm{CH_3-N}$.

Draw structures for two possible products when this nitrene from $\mathrm{CH_3-N_3}$ reacts with ethylene gas ($\mathrm{CH_2CH_2}$).

Photoresists consisting of Novolak polymers use acid to change their solubility. The acid component can be produced photochemically from diazonaphthaquinone. “Novolaks” have been the representative “positive” photoresists of the modern microelectronic revolution.

![](p9-fig2)

When irradiated, diazonaphthaquinone undergoes photochemical decomposition followed by rearrangement eventually producing a carboxylic acid.

![](p9-fig3)

Draw three Lewis structures of diazoacetaldehyde (below), the simplest compound having the same active functional group as diazonaphthaquinone. Indicate formal charges.

![](p9-fig4)

Draw a Lewis structure of the rearranged intermediate A (below), generated from diazoacetaldehyde after losing $\mathrm{N_2}$. A satisfies Lewis' octet rule and reacts with water to form acetic acid, $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$.

![](p9-fig5)

Advanced photoresists were invented in 1982 based on chemical amplification. The most popular amplification for positive-tone involves acid-catalyzed deprotection of poly(p-hydroxystyrene) resin protected by various acid-sensitive groups such as t-butyloxycarbonyl (t-BOC).

![](p9-fig6)

The thermal decomposition of carbonate ester itself normally occurs well above $150\ ^\circ\mathrm C$.

Two plausible mechanisms have been suggested for this decomposition reaction having relatively high activation energy. Draw expected intermediates and products from this reaction.

![](p9-fig7)

In the presence of a trace amount of acid, the reaction temperature can be reduced below $100\ ^\circ\mathrm C$. Draw expected intermediate F from the following chemical-amplification process based on t-BOC.

![](p9-fig8)
